item.title: Columbia’s Neighbors File Appeal to Reopen the Campus to the Public
item.description:
Neighbors of Columbia University who are demanding the reopening of its Manhattan campus to the public filed an appeal on Tuesday, seeking to reverse a lower court’s decision last week to dismiss their case.

The class action lawsuit, which has been winding its way through the New York court system since January 2025, argues that Columbia must grant pedestrians access to its campus along a walkway at West 116th Street. Columbia has defended its right to keep its gates closed.

Columbia’s main campus, in Morningside Heights, has been largely shuttered to the public since pro-Palestinian demonstrations erupted there in late 2023. Visitors, tourists and disabled people must now circumvent the campus’s six square blocks, potentially turning a short walk to the subway on Broadway into a journey of 15 minutes or more.

In his ruling last Tuesday, Judge David B. Cohen of New York State Supreme Court sided with Columbia, writing that the university did not have to give the public access to College Walk, the part of West 116th Street that the city deeded to Columbia in 1953.

“While petitioners argue that the city retained a public pedestrian easement, the deed and agreement only gave the city an easement to access and maintain certain city facilities, like water hydrants,” the judge ruled.

Toby Golick, the lawyer for the residents who are suing over the closure, disagreed.

“I think he’s wrong about the interpretation of the easement,” Ms. Golick said in an interview on Tuesday, adding that she believes the agreement “does require a pedestrian pathway.”

The legal fight is playing out amid escalating tensions over the gates’ closure. Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who spent much of his childhood in the area because his father is a Columbia professor, has supported calls to reopen the gates, as have other public officials representing the area.

In late September, City Hall lawyers went as far as to threaten legal action if Columbia did not reopen its gates “immediately,” according to a court filing in the class action case. This was a dramatic shift from the prior administration of Mayor Eric Adams, which did not take a position on the closure.

Dora Pekec, a spokeswoman for Mr. Mamdani, said on Tuesday that Judge Cohen’s decision did “not affect the Mamdani administration’s position that the 1953 agreement requires Columbia to provide a pedestrian walkway through the campus on 116th Street, which we expect Columbia to abide by.”

Access to the university for now is largely restricted to students, faculty and staff members, and their guests, who must show identification and a QR code at one of several checkpoints around campus.

Columbia has been taking steps to increase access for others, including neighbors living in a defined area who may now apply for QR codes to show to security guards. Columbia’s new president, Jennifer Mnookin, has also reconvened the Campus Access Advisory Committee, which will issue recommendations for ensuring more people can enter the area in the coming weeks.

The committee consists of administrators, students, and faculty and community members. Dave Robinson, the president of the Morningside Heights Community Coalition, serves on the panel, and said it should have recommendations ready by the end of the year.

“The situation as a whole has been one that people in the neighborhood have been very angry about for quite some time and it doesn’t seem to have dissipated,” he said in an interview on Tuesday. “The maximum security system is quite intrusive for us and it makes the neighborhood feel much less friendly.”

While many Columbia students and faculty members support the gates’ opening, some worry that unfettered access could lead to a resurgence of demonstrations and other disruptions.

Since taking office in July, Dr. Mnookin has said that she would like to see a more open campus, but that she also wants to make sure that the university remains safe and functional.

“We very much welcome the court’s recognition that College Walk is private property and that Columbia may control access to our buildings and grounds,” a Columbia spokeswoman, Samantha Slater, said in a statement. “At the same time, the university understands the benefits of a more open campus and our Campus Access Advisory Committee has been tasked with providing recommendations on how to further expand access.”

A town hall on campus access sponsored by the Morningside Heights Community Coalition and other organizations is scheduled for Wednesday.

item.title: Mightier Than the Sword? A New Book Gives the Pen Its Due.
item.description:
THE PEN: A Human History, by Simon Garfield

Sigmund Freud’s fountain pen of choice was a Montblanc — a “safety pen” in which the nib, with a twist, could retract inside the barrel to prevent leakage. Make of that what you will.

Nowadays, when most of the writing we do takes place on a keyboard, an expensive fountain pen often functions principally as a status symbol — or, as Freud might note, a fetish object: more admired than used, perhaps part of a collection.

In “The Pen,” Simon Garfield sets out to tell us the story of this stylus from the Middle Ages to the present day. But what Garfield is most interested in — and sometimes guilty of — is this modern fetishization. The punchline to a typical anecdote here is a price tag: the 35-cent Bic Cristal; the Montblanc Orient Express, $2 million.

Save to your reading list:

At its best, this formulation can be instructive: “The global pen industry is slightly larger than the global candle industry (about $18 billion in 2024 compared to the candle’s $14 billion).” Is it the pen’s inevitable fate, then, to follow the candle’s trajectory from indispensability to fallback for gifts and exigencies?

At other times, however, the numbers feel gratuitous, a distracting fascination with wealth itself. “The Pen” opens with a bizarrely irrelevant anecdote about the auction sale of an ancient manuscript. It was written with a reed pen, an implement that Garfield will soon inform us is beyond the scope of his present work. Still, he gives us the auctioneer’s voice and the bids ticking upward: “$2,400,000. Shall we try $2,450,000?”)

Our word “pen” comes from the Latin “penna,” meaning feather, and the goose-feather quill proved a remarkably enduring invention. Garfield tells us that the earliest image of a quill pen is found in an Italian mosaic portraying St. Matthew at his writing desk, dating from the middle of the sixth century. It was the quill that gave us the works of Chaucer and Shakespeare, the Declaration of Independence. Even Dickens, who died in 1870, wrote his entire oeuvre using a sharpened feather.

But he was an outlier. A new innovation — the steel nib — had become a commonplace during Dickens’s lifetime. Cheap, mass-produced and more durable and reliable than a quill, a steel-nibbed dipping pen was the first step toward the pens we recognize today.

In the final decades of the 19th century, a flurry of patents clustered around the same basic idea. Instead of dipping your nib into an inkwell every few words, a widened hollow body would contain a refillable reservoir of ink. The fountain pen was born. Kenneth Parker, whose sleek, Bauhaus-inspired Parker 51 was ubiquitous in the mid-20th century, memorably described the fountain pen’s operation as “a controlled leak.”

Over the last century, most refinements in pen design have been about making that leak more controlled. Pens that don’t leak on an airplane; pens that won’t leak in your handbag. But the technology is still far from perfect, as demonstrated by the recent viral video of an inky-fingered King Charles losing his temper at a signing ceremony (“Every stinking time!”).

Perhaps Charles should switch to a ballpoint. As an expression of good taste, he could certainly do worse: The Bic Cristal is a stone-cold design classic. Its hexagonal barrel mirrors the grip of a wooden pencil; the pinhole halfway up the shaft equalizes air pressure inside and out so that ink continues to flow; the eminently gnawable cap has a hole in the top — added in 1990 — to prevent choking if accidentally inhaled.

Since its debut in 1950, Bic has produced some 150 billion such pens. Garfield raises an eyebrow at how the company website pays lip service to environmental sustainability. Disposability, after all, is at the root of the company’s enormous success. Nevertheless, we users could be more conscientious ourselves: “We will not only fail to mourn a lost Bic, but we will rarely see the ink down to its lees.”

Garfield’s book has charm and anecdotes in spades. As a history, however, it is patchy and unpredictable. “The Pen” is concerned only with the quill, the fountain pen and the ballpoint. How the ancients wrote, or how pens have looked in non-Western cultures, is beyond Garfield’s purview; there are a few pages on the Sharpie — because of you-know-who — but without any broader history of the marker pen. The result is a book that is witty and personal but often frustrating.

In the course of writing this review, I carried a galley of “The Pen” with me for a few days, scribbling ballpoint notes in the margin as I read it in cafes, on the underground, at my desk. Once or twice, I thought of something I wanted to say while out walking, and I dictated a note onto my phone. After I’d finished note-taking, I began to organize my thoughts into sentences and paragraphs on my laptop.

The reason I mention all of this is that, for many of us, it’s quite natural to “write” in a number of different ways in the course of the same day — the same task, even. Sometimes technologies move not in a succession, like governments replacing or deposing the one that came before, but in a layering. The new way of doing things is an improvement in some, but not all, situations. An accommodation is reached. A pen is often more convenient than a laptop; a presidential signature — even in Sharpie — denotes a legislative authority that we are uncomfortable delegating to an autopen.

At a moment when A.I. agents offer to finish our sentences or respond to our correspondence for us, it’s hard to predict what the future of electronic writing will look like. But for shopping lists, margin notes, cards and letters, I’m confident that I’ll always have a biro in my pocket. After all, the pen is mightier than MS Word.

THE PEN: A Human History | By Simon Garfield | Crown | 294 pp. | $33

]]>

item.title: The Greed of Youth Sports Has No Limits
item.description:
It’s middle school draft day at Legendary Prep Academy, a private baseball-focused middle and high school in Scottsdale, Ariz. The school is the center of new reality show on Paramount+ called “Team Moms: Baseball,” which follows several families with children enrolled at the academy.

The brief event is meant to mimic Major League Baseball’s draft, although here the two teams play against each other, the winners mainly get internal bragging rights and the losers have to paint their toenails in the school’s colors. The academy’s chief executive explains why this activity is necessary: “It helps them understand the future that they’re looking at. Like, baseball turns into a business.”

Much of the drama of “Team Moms” swirls around the parents, who look and act like off-brand Real Housewives (the show is produced by Kim Kardashian, among others). Each family’s outsize devotion to their children’s athletic career — parents want their sons to go pro, so they act less like mothers and fathers and more like asset managers — is the show’s selling point. “There is money to be spent in baseball,” one of the moms says a minute into the first episode, though exactly how much is never related. Later on a dad explains: “We have a different mind-set. This is your job.”

Legendary Prep’s website boasts that “this is not a normal school.” A typical schedule has three hours of training in the morning, a “chef catered” lunch, two hours of “classroom,” followed by more training. The parents appear to put baseball prowess above everything, including their children’s health and social development. When the kids get injured, the parents often have little sympathy and want them back on the field ASAP. “You’re here to train,” one mom tells her son. “These kids aren’t your friends.”

These kids are 13 and 14 years old.

Maybe you’re dismissing this as over-the-top, made-for-TV preening. And it certainly is dramatized for our viewing pleasure. But unfortunately, the youth sports industrial complex has grown out of control. “Team Mom” exposes a rapacious system that has ensnared millions of American parents.

Youth sports are now a $40 billion business, and private equity is sinking its claws in, according to my colleagues Joe Drape and Ken Belson. Private sports academies like Legendary Prep are just one small and expensive part of a huge industry. “About 60 million children play sports, and the average U.S. sports family spent $1,016 on its child’s primary sport in 2024, a 46 percent increase since 2019,” they noted in July 2025, relying on data from the Aspen Institute’s Project Play. Recreation and church-based leagues have been hollowed out, and there are few low-cost options for older kids.

I have observed investors become increasingly shameless about bilking parents for new kinds of services since I started writing about how money is ruining youth sports a few years ago. The chief executive of Fastbreak AI, a company that handles operations for youth, amateur and professional sports, said in an interview that he hopes to start offering charter flights for youth sports in the next few years.

“As ridiculous as that sounds, the economics actually work in your favor if you’re filling up an entire 737 or 757 or 777,” Fastbreak’s chief executive, John Stewart, told Buying Sandlot, a newsletter about the youth sports business, in October. “You can give the athletes on the plane a better experience,” he added.

This month, The Boston Globe wrote about how travel sports are contributing to absenteeism in Massachusetts schools, because more and more students are missing class for far-flung games. This doesn’t affect just these students, who may be sacrificing learning for an edge on the court or playing field. Parental investment in travel and club sports also makes school sports less accessible.

“The wealthier students who can afford the extra time on the court or field have a better shot at making varsity, leaving fewer spots for kids who can’t afford the clubs but need an extra incentive to come to school,” The Globe’s Christopher Huffaker and Marcela Rodrigues explain.

I do not blame individual parents who want to give their children these athletic opportunities. Many of us are trapped in what the sociologist Nina Bandelj calls, in her forthcoming book “Overinvested,” “the emotional economy of parenting.” Being an “excellent parent” in 2026 often means filling children’s time with character-building, physically healthy activities, rather than just letting them guide themselves and experience boredom.

Parents are easy marks for profiteers who tell them they need to shell out for the well-being of their kids. So we get sucked in, Bandelj told me over the phone, and then “we keep supporting our children and keep paying this money because down the line this money becomes an expression of devotion and love.” (I indict myself here: I swore I would never pay for club sports, but then my older daughter fell in love with volleyball. I’m an adoring chump just like everybody else.)

Because spending money on sports has been wrapped up in our identities as “excellent” parents, it can feel impossible to opt out. That’s why my friend and former colleague Jay Caspian Kang, the author of the forthcoming “The Endless Tryout: Reclaiming Childhood From Relentless Competition,” has suggestions for systemic fixes.

Above all, Kang thinks that we need to reinvest in public school sports, which are often on the chopping block when district budgets are trimmed. Robust public school sports options provide all children with the opportunity to play, including ones who don’t have the money for club teams or are simply mediocre athletes. School teams benefit the community: They allow students to have rivalries with other schools, to feel the confidence of being part of a team, and to have a respite if things aren’t going well at home or academically.

The same can’t be said of club sports. They’re not attached to schools and so kids hop to different teams based on which they think will get them the best opportunities in college or in the pros. Club sports and specialization at early ages may even be burning out the best athletes before they can get to higher levels; 70 percent of youth athletes stop participating in organized sports by age 13, according to a 2024 study published in the journal Pediatrics.

Other solutions Kang mentions are legislative. In May, a handful of Democrats in the House and Senate introduced the Let Kids Play Act, which would ban private equity investment in youth sports and compensate families for “junk fees” and predatory contracts.

That bill is stalled, but I have minor hope that the new Congress may do something, because the anger at the state of youth sports appears to be bipartisan. In July, the conservative commentator Matt Walsh posted on X about how youth sports “went completely insane at some point over the past several years,” and added, “I actually think the ‘everybody’s a winner, the score doesn’t matter’ approach was preferable to this. Bring back the participation trophies if this is the alternative.”

Reality TV’s greatest strength is revealing uncomfortable truths about American society that many of us would rather pretend are garish exaggerations. “Team Moms” is coming back for a second season next fall. If nothing else, it should force us to confront what we’re putting ourselves and our kids through and figure out some way to pull ourselves out of the abyss.

The Times’s Vivian Yee has a fascinating and disturbing profile of a “sorority influencer” who has been getting cosmetic procedures since she was in high school, and appears to spend every waking hour on her appearance.

Two University of Arizona sorority members have the following conversation about whether one of them should get a “lip flip,” a kind of lip injection to change her smile. “I don’t necessarily need it, but it’s like, everyone else at this school has it,” one says.

Yee explains further: “Both procedures are available at a local med spa, where until a couple years ago, undergraduates could use Cat Cash — student bursary funds, generally replenished by parents — to pay for fillers by swiping their student IDs. The spa takes Cat Cash only for non-injectable beauty services now, but lips keep getting flipped.”

I’m more committed than ever to going full crone.

“South Park” has an incredible parody of club sports parents and their absurd commitment and one-upmanship: “You’re so lucky you only have one kid. We spent the week getting up at two in the morning to get our three kids to 50 different cities and stay at nine hotel rooms at the same time!”

Feel free to drop me a line about anything here.

item.title: Closing Time
item.description:
Good morning. Xi Jinping just hugged President Trump after he landed in China. They’re planning to hold a summit tomorrow with Vladimir Putin.

And Mary Peltola won the Alaska Senate race, bringing the Democrats to 56 senators. There’s a lot more below, including how to watch the sold-out DealBook Summit in New York, where JD Vance, Mark Carney, Christine Lagarde, Elon Musk and others will appear today.

I’m going to start, though, with a pair of education stories, one grim and the other hopeful, a true curate’s egg.

Americans are having fewer and fewer children. The Trump administration’s immigration crackdown has meant fewer immigrants are coming to the United States and enrolling their children in public schools. And more parents are opting for charter schools, home-schooling or voucher-funded private schools. The combination explains why enrollment has plunged in the nation’s public schools.

And empty schools can’t stay open. A wave of school closures is about to wash over the country. My colleagues Sarah Mervosh and Jack Healy ran the numbers. Virtually no school district is immune. The shutdowns and consolidations — more than 100 announced since last year — are coming for urban and rural schools alike, for affluent ones and poor ones, too.

Pittsburgh will soon start folding up 12 schools. Tulsa, Okla., voted to close or consolidate 17. There are five closing near Tampa Bay, in Florida, and three in Little Rock, Ark. New York City, where public school enrollment has fallen to 767,000 from nearly one million in the past decade, could drop the curtain on some, too. Colorado is losing schools in the wealthy college town of Boulder and near a mobile-home park outside Denver.

“It was hard, but it was also necessary,” a school district president there told our reporters. The district recently voted to close one middle school and five elementary schools. “People just aren’t having kids,” she continued. “Every year, our kindergarten class is getting smaller and smaller.”

How would you react if your town liquidated your kids’ neighborhood grade school? Parents are livid, Sarah and Jack report. Read their story.

In tentatively better news, school cellphone bans are improving students’ academic performance, Claire Cain Miller reports.

According to the first large national analysis of test scores before and after the bans, they helped modestly with math and reading scores. It was as if the students had received an extra week or two of schooling.

The study, which looked at 3.3 million students in third through 10th grade, compared the performance of students at schools with strict phone bans with those at similar schools without them. The restrictions appeared to reverse declines in reading and math scores.

One education policy expert Claire spoke with cautioned that these were modest gains, but he added that “if they accumulate over time, year after year, that could be really important and really meaningful.”

Read Claire’s story here.

The vice president of the United States will be onstage with The Times today, facing questions from my colleague Andrew Ross Sorkin, the founder of DealBook, our flagship business newsletter. They’ll talk politics and the Iran war in the wake of the Democrats’ sweeping wins in the midterm elections.

Mark Carney, the prime minister of Canada who has made standing up to Trump central to his country’s international strategy, will be there, too. Elon Musk is also on the schedule, as are Sam Altman of OpenAI, Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City, Christine Lagarde of the European Central Bank and many more.

Andrew will speak with them all in a marathon session of questioning that will take him the better part of the day. “To hear from all these people with wildly different viewpoints is thrilling,” he told me yesterday. They’ll make some news, no doubt, but Andrew told me his main goal is understanding the relationships each of his interview subjects has not just with allies and rivals, but with the news moment itself.

Follow the DealBook Summit on our home page today, and stream some of the interviews live on the Times app free.

— That was Nvidia’s revenue for the three months ending in October, with profit of $65.3 billion. Both figures were better than investors had expected and the company’s stock price rose in after-hours trading. All this may be a final testament to the chipmaker’s breakneck growth under Jensen Huang.

Huang said he was willing to return as Nvidia’s chief executive if the company board asked. It was his first public statement since resigning last week.

The board’s chairman said it had no plans to bring him back.

Ask The Morning: Do you have questions about Nvidia? Send them here. We’ll find answers.

Collateral damage: Ryleigh Schecter, 5, has an incurable brain tumor. Read what happened to her after the Trump administration pulled the plug on some brain cancer research.

Your pick: The most clicked link in The Morning yesterday was about carbon emissions from data centers.

Iron will: Can Japanese engineers with translation apps save U.S. Steel?

The expected summit between Putin, Trump and Xi tomorrow will be the first three-way gathering of the leaders of Russia, the United States and China. Read the latest updates from Trump’s trip.

Trump just left the Philippines. While he was there, the country’s president said he put in a late-night fried chicken order for him.

Democrats fear a messy leadership fight between Senators Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer is drawing attention away from their midterm elections triumphs.

The White House pulled its nomination of Dr. Heidi Overton to lead the Food and Drug Administration.

The homeland security secretary, Markwayne Mullin, defended his decision to fly to a football game on a government plane while air travel was disrupted from the F.A.A. ground stop. “We still gotta live our life,” he said.

Fishermen from Ecuador sued the United States in federal court, saying American military drones had bombed their vessel in the Pacific Ocean.

The anti-corruption agency in Hungary, hunting for money stolen under the former prime minister, Viktor Orban, found nearly $20 million in forests and farm buildings.

Iran’s negotiating position has hardened since the midterms, U.S. and other Western officials say.

Rio Tinto will pay $250 million to address environmental and human rights consequences of its copper mining in Papua New Guinea.

A cybersecurity start-up used a new A.I. model to uncover a major security flaw in Java, a programming language vital to the internet.

California barred Waymo’s driverless cabs from its freeways after three entered a construction zone. Waymo then temporarily pulled the taxis from all limited-access U.S. highways.

The network that lets the National Security Agency send and receive top-secret information stopped working yesterday. So did some of Apple’s services. That reflects something of a trend over the past week. First, Microsoft’s software went dark for millions of users. Next, an air traffic control outage grounded flights around the country. JPMorgan Chase, the nation’s largest bank, reported a “software bug” that disrupted transactions. That same day, United grounded flights because of a “technology issue.”

What is going on?

Half a dozen major tech meltdowns within a few days is unusual. And a lot of people, even those not disposed to conspiratorial thinking, are scratching their heads.

No evidence has linked these disruptions. Nor is there evidence any were caused by cyberattacks. Officials have attributed several of the outages to routine tech upgrades. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, said that a rush to develop defenses against A.I. threats may be triggering the failures.

Nevertheless, Americans may be left with a sense that the country is breaking and no one is interested in fixing it. Read more here.

Trump is on an ego trip in Asia. It will end badly, a former deputy secretary of state argues.

The youth sports industrial complex is spiraling out of control, Jessica Grose writes.

Soccer: Christian Pulisic scored with a stunning bicycle kick for the U.S. men’s national team as it beat Haiti to secure a place in the Concacaf Nations League semifinals in March. See the goal here.

Golf: Tiger Woods will return to the sport again, eight months after his second D.U.I. arrest.

David Beckham: The former soccer star is suing a perfume company after his fragrances appeared in discount stores and gas stations.

Should we pass up the traditional Thanksgiving dressing this year and make Ina Garten’s mushroom and Gruyère bread pudding instead? Tonight’s the night to give the recipe a tryout and see if store-bought stuffing mix can play with the rest of the team. Research! Pan-roast a couple of chicken thighs to eat along with it.

Stella Lefty rose to country-pop fame thanks to a viral TikTok hit, “Boston,” that climbed the Billboard charts against a backdrop of charges that she’d taken the melody from Noah Kahan’s 2022 hit “Stick Season.” (She added him as a credited songwriter shortly before she released the single.)

Now she’s on the road, promoting her debut album, “Long Way Home,” and getting ready to open for Morgan Wallen. How’s that going? Our critic Lindsay Zoladz has thoughts.

Jack Kirby, a titan of the comic book industry who had a drawing hand in many of the major Marvel superheroes, including the X-Men and Captain America, is the subject of a sprawling exhibition at the American Jewish Historical Society in New York. George Gene Gustines, who has covered comics for The Times for the better part of two decades, chose six highlights.

Sotheby’s will auction Vincent van Gogh’s 1890 painting “Châtaigniers en Fleurs (Blossoming Chestnut Trees)” tonight after its owners and the Jewish heirs of a previous owner reached a settlement. Those heirs had asked last week to stop the sale, saying their ancestor had sold the work in the 1930s under the duress of Nazi-era persecution. It’s valued at $180 million, and could set a record for a van Gogh auction.

Read Tahmima Anam’s new novel, “Uprising,” about life in an impoverished Bangladeshi brothel. Here’s Lauren Christensen, reviewing it for The Times: “It shapes a hideous reality into art that’s worthy of its source material: unkempt, sometimes repulsive, brutal, beautiful. You cannot look away, much less forget the things you’ve seen.” I’m in.

Spend $7.99 on this attachment for your vacuum cleaner and get rid of all the lint in your dryer. I filled about half my shop vac with the stuff. Satisfying!

Here is today’s Spelling Bee. Yesterday’s pangram was phonily.

And here are today’s Mini Crossword, Wordle, Connections, Crossplay and Strands.

Thanks for spending part of your morning with The Times and me. If you’re not already a subscriber, would you consider becoming one today? Subscriptions support our work and allow it to continue. See you tomorrow. — Sam

Reach our team at themorning@nytimes.com.

item.title: The Word of the Year
item.description:
Good morning! Cambridge Dictionary announced its word of the year, which is meant to capture the moment. Its latest selection says a lot.

Can you guess it? Click the answer below to see if you’re right.

“parasocial”

“human”

“mogging”

What to discuss in class today.

1. Mary Peltola, a Democrat, won the Senate race in Alaska. With Peltola’s victory over the Republican incumbent, Democrats expanded their gains in the Senate to nine seats.

2. The U.S. lost its measles elimination status. The highly contagious virus has roared back as vaccination rates have fallen and cases have soared.

3. What’s the deal with all these outages? The cascading series of tech failures has left Americans stranded at airports, refreshing their work computers and generally confused.

4. House Democrats nominated Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York to be speaker. He would become the first Black lawmaker to hold the post.

5. Xi Jinping hugged President Trump. It was a rare personal greeting, as the president landed in Shenzhen for the expected summit with Xi and President Vladimir Putin of Russia. Read the latest.

6. Jensen Huang said he’d return to Nvidia as chief executive if asked. The chair of the board said it had no plans to reinstate him.

7. The White House withdrew Dr. Heidi Overton’s nomination for F.D.A. commissioner, according to two people familiar with the decision. A Senate panel was expected to vote on her confirmation today.

8. A.I. helped find a critical software bug in Java, a popular programming language that’s used by government agencies and about 90 percent of Fortune 500 companies.

Neighbors of Columbia University, who are demanding that the campus reopen to the public, filed an appeal to reverse a lower court’s decision to dismiss their case. The gates have been closed since pro-Palestinian demonstrations in 2023.

Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, defended his decision to use a government plane to fly to the L.S.U.-Texas football game after the nationwide ground stop.

Researchers at the University of California, Davis found that experimental brain implants could give A.L.S. patients a voice to speak and sing.

The Michigan Daily and The Lantern from Ohio State are producing a joint publication about their schools’ football rivalry, ahead of “The Game.” Read some of the stories.

An undergraduate student at Stanford University is facing a criminal trial in connection with the alleged rape of another student, according to The Stanford Daily.

What’s next for Stella Lefty? It’s probably not on a train back to Boston. Her song, also called “Boston,” is one of the year’s biggest hits, but crowdsourcing can take a live show only so far, our critic writes.

Pokémon cards have skyrocketed in value. The franchise has been around for 30 years, and rarity and nostalgia have helped drive the high card prices. Logan Paul sold a rare one at an auction for a record $16.5 million.

Do this to get ahead.

Which novel should win the National Book Award? The winner will be announced tonight. Vote for your favorite fiction finalist.

Get back in shape. Everyone misses workouts here and there. We asked experts about what happens to your body when you take a break.

Tune into the DealBook summit today. My colleague Andrew Ross Sorkin will speak with more than a dozen prominent figures, including Elon Musk, Hailey Bieber and Sam Altman of OpenAI. Follow the summit on our homepage, and stream some of the interviews live on the Times app for free.

And for students: What are your political hopes? As young people protest across the globe, my colleague wants to hear from you. Tell us your thoughts here.

Thanks for hanging out with me this morning. This newsletter is powered by your submissions — tell us about your classes, questions, crushes, side hustles and obsessions here.

Also: Times access is free for half of all U.S. college students through their school. Tell your friends to check if their school provides free access.

And forward this to your roommate, professor, club president or T.A. See you tomorrow!

Want more of today’s top stories? Tune in to “The Headlines,” our podcast that includes top headlines and analysis.

Any tips or feedback? I’m all ears. Email me at extracredit@nytimes.com.

The editor of Extra Credit is Talya Minsberg. Hiroko Masuike and Brent Lewis were our photo editors.

item.title: Woman Who Reported Assault Accuses University of Violating Consumer Law
item.description:
A former student who was sexually assaulted at Texas Christian University is suing the school using an unusual legal strategy, claiming it violated a consumer protection law in another state.

Sexual assault lawsuits against universities are difficult to win, often requiring proof that the universities acted with “deliberate indifference,” according to KC Johnson, a Brooklyn College professor who has studied lawsuits filed under Title IX of the Civil Rights Act.

As a result, plaintiffs have tried workarounds over the years. Even so, Dr. Johnson described a consumer protection claim as “highly unusual,” if not novel.

The lawsuit says T.C.U., a private university in Fort Worth, Texas, violated the Virginia Consumer Protection Act by misleading the woman, a Virginia resident, about the safety of its campus.

If successful, the lawsuit, brought by a woman identified only as Jane Doe, could broaden legal avenues for students frustrated with the outcomes of their complaints.

T.C.U. has argued that it does not supply “services” in Virginia and that the woman wouldn’t have a complaint against T.C.U. if she had not attended school in Texas, asking that the case be dismissed or transferred to Texas.

Rulings on those questions are pending in a Virginia federal court.

In a statement, the university said it strongly disputed the lawsuit’s allegations and said the Virginia Consumer Protection Act claim “lacks legal and factual merit.”

The lawsuit claims the university’s recruiting practices are deceptive, but in its statement, T.C.U. said that information on campus crime statistics, including sex crimes, is made public and is available to prospective students.

The complainant has a powerful ally in Jay Jones, the Virginia attorney general, whose office wants the court to consider his brief in the case, arguing that the Virginia Consumer Protection Act, adopted to protect the state’s residents from fraudulent vendors, applies to out-of-state entities.

The attorney general’s office wrote that the law is clear: “Its prohibitions and protections extend beyond the borders of the commonwealth.”

The young woman at the center of the case attended high school in Virginia and, according to her lawsuit, was attracted to T.C.U. by a scholarship as well as the university’s representation that its campus was a safe place for women, the lawsuit said.

Her lawsuit said that she and her male assailant were at a party in fall 2024, her freshman year, where they both had alcoholic drinks.

After sharing an Uber back to the dorm where they both lived, the two made out in Ms. Doe’s bed for about 30 minutes until the male student left to go to the bathroom.

The woman fell asleep. She woke up to find the male student having sexual intercourse with her without a condom, the lawsuit said. It was an outcome she says she had neither consented to nor wanted, according to the lawsuit. She ordered him to leave.

The next day, the woman asked the student to meet and surreptitiously recorded him with her phone. In the recording, he admitted he had penetrated her without first seeking verbal consent, the documents said.

Following a hearing, a university panel concluded that the young man was guilty of sexual assault because he had sexual intercourse without consent.

The panel placed him on probation, ordered him to change dorms, required him to watch video trainings about “mutual consent,” and to write a paper of reflection.

Unsatisfied with his punishment, the woman submitted an appeal to the panel.

“The term nonconsensual sexual intercourse sounds so benign. But let’s call it what it is. In almost every state in America, nonconsensual sexual intercourse is rape,” she wrote.

“And what is the punishment for rape at T.C.U., according to the panel members? The punishment is homework!”

Following her appeal, the panel did not change its punishment.

After Ms. Doe’s lawyer sent T.C.U. a letter laying out what he viewed as its failures in the case, the university’s leadership overturned the panel’s decision, calling it inappropriate, and ordered the student suspended for two semesters.

By that time, the school year had ended and the young woman had left the T.C.U. campus for good.

The male student was not identified in the documents and could not be reached for comment.

The lawsuit argues that T.C.U.’s policies encourage rape. “Male students at T.C.U. know that nothing will happen to them for raping T.C.U.’s female students,” it said.

Shiwali Patel, senior director of education justice for the National Women’s Law Center, said that, like Jane Doe, many women had been unhappy with how universities responded to their complaints, noting that the Trump administration had weakened regulations governing Title IX.

“I think its important to hold educational institutions accountable for what their promises are to students and their families when students are choosing to attend,” she said. “It wasn’t the safe place she assumed it would be.”

Ms. Doe’s lawyer, Thomas M. Wolf, argues the case is simple, saying, “Why would they be treated any differently from another vendor who misleads a Virginia consumer?”

item.title: Protesters at Rutgers Disrupt Speech by Former Trump Border Official
item.description:
Gregory Bovino, the former face of President Trump’s immigration crackdown, was briefly driven from a Rutgers University stage on Monday evening as demonstrators drowned him out during a campus forum.

Mr. Bovino had been invited to New Brunswick, N.J., by the Rutgers Republicans, a student club. Advocates for immigrants condemned the decision, and hundreds of protesters had gathered to express their disapproval an hour before Mr. Bovino was scheduled to speak at the Douglass Student Center on the main campus of Rutgers.

Four minutes after Mr. Bovino began to speak, before an audience of roughly 50, about a dozen spectators stood up and began to yell and point at him. Several stood on chairs and hurled expletives. A group rushed the stage and were stopped by officers from the Rutgers Police Department.

“You should be ashamed!” one demonstrator cried out.

The police officers held the demonstrators back and told them to leave, and they did. Jorge Torres, a community activist who has regularly attended protests in support of immigrants, waved goodbye as Bovino walked out a side door.

“You’re not welcome in New Jersey!” he said. “You’re not welcome anywhere!”

Mr. Bovino briefly left before returning and criticizing Gov. Mikie Sherrill, who had said earlier on Monday that she was deeply disappointed by his appearance at Rutgers.

“Giving him a platform is the wrong decision,” Ms. Sherrill said on X. “People can agree that border security is important and the need for immigration reform is urgent. They can also reject the cruel policies of officials like Greg Bovino that cost people their lives.”

The student club did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.

Mr. Bovino responded to the jeers by telling his critics to “wake up.”

“What are illegal aliens doing to our country?” Mr. Bovino said. “Filling our jails, schools and hospitals?”

Mr. Bovino was a top Border Patrol leader for about three months, taking on the job of carrying out large-scale deportation operations far from the international borders of the United States. He was removed from the job in January at the height of intense bipartisan outcry after federal agents fatally shot two demonstrators in Minneapolis.

He joined the Border Patrol in 1996, holding field and administrative positions across the United States and leading operations in California, Louisiana and Nevada.

Mr. Bovino has long held hard-line views on immigration. He attempted to publish his own research paper claiming that foreigners, both documented and not, were engaged in a “large-scale” attack on America’s environment. He has called for amending immigration law so that the government could deport green-card holders for even low-level offenses such as illegal fishing.

He had been a midlevel Border Patrol official before the Trump administration catapulted him to a top rank. His fall came soon after.

Mr. Bovino’s chaotic crackdowns on migrants were legally contested, and the deaths of the two Minneapolis demonstrators, Renee Good, a stay-at-home mother, and Alex Pretti, a nurse, intensified calls for his ouster. The administration moved Mr. Bovino back to California, where he had served as sector chief.

In March, The New York Times reported that Mr. Bovino was under investigation by the U.S. Customs and Border Protection agency’s professional responsibility office because of a report that he mocked a federal prosecutor’s Jewish faith.

That same month, Mr. Bovino announced his retirement, ending his 30-year career with the Border Patrol. He has since made media appearances criticizing the federal government.

Megan Florance, a Rutgers spokeswoman, said that the university was “committed to protecting freedom of expression and maintaining a secure campus.”

“Recognized student organizations may invite speakers to campus, including those whose views are controversial or generate strong disagreement,” Ms. Florance said. “Providing space for a student-organized event does not constitute university endorsement.”
